=== 2025-12-19 58481 - ERCOT Comments on Discussion.docx ===
Project No. 58481


ELECTRIC RELIABILITY COUNCIL OF TEXAS, INC.’S 
COMMENTS ON DISCUSSION DRAFT

Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc. (ERCOT) respectfully submits these comments to Public Utility Commission of Texas (Commission) Staff’s December 1, 2025 discussion draft of proposed rule 16 Tex. Admin. Code (TAC) § 25.194, regarding large load interconnection standards.  These comments also include responses to Commission Staff’s questions 1, 2, and 3 in the discussion draft.
COMMENTS ON DISCUSSION DRAFT
Revisions to the draft rule may be necessary to accommodate a batch study process for large load interconnections.
At the Commission’s December 18, 2025 open meeting, ERCOT announced that it intends to propose a “batch study” process for studying interconnections of large loads instead of the existing process that requires a separate evaluation of each large load’s transmission system impacts.  The primary purpose of this new batch study process would be to increase the overall efficiency and speed of large load integration by eliminating the need to restart the study process for a given large load each time another proposed load in the study area meets the criteria for being included in the study cases.  As the number of large loads seeking interconnection has grown exponentially, the frequency of restudies has increased commensurately, quickly becoming one of the most significant obstacles to moving large load development forward in the ERCOT Region.  
The recent implementation of Planning Guide Revision Request (PGRR) 115—which codifies ERCOT’s large load interconnection process—is expected to reduce the incidence of restudy to some degree by strengthening the criteria used to determine when a proposed load triggers a restudy of other proposed loads in the same area.  However, it will not entirely eliminate the risk of restudy; projects that meet these higher criteria will continue to trigger restudies for other nearby projects.  
A batch study process could solve this restudy problem by eliminating load-specific studies in favor of a single, periodic batch study conducted at regular intervals (possibly semiannually) that would include all large loads meeting certain commitment and/or development criteria within a specified time window.  Under this new process, when a load meets the criteria for inclusion in the batch study, this would no longer trigger new studies for other loads; it would simply result in the inclusion of that load in the next batch study.  
In addition to eliminating the need for restudies, a batch study process would provide both a more accurate assessment of the aggregate transmission system impacts of the large loads in the study and a more accurate identification of the transmission system upgrades needed to accommodate those loads compared to the existing individual study process.  By including only those large loads that meet the required commitment and development criteria, these studies would provide a much greater level of confidence in the transmission upgrades ERCOT identifies as needed.  Additionally, a batch study process that includes a concept of capacity reservation could provide greater certainty to committed loads that the transmission capacity identified in the studies will be available to those loads when they energize.  Today, no such reservation process exists.  ERCOT believes that a capacity reservation concept would align closely with Commission Staff’s proposal in subsection (h)(9)(B) of the discussion draft to require each large load customer to pay a contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) that would include not only the costs of the direct interconnection facilities but also the costs of system upgrades attributable to the customer.  
As discussed at the December 18, 2025 open meeting, development of this new study process will require close collaboration with Commission Staff and significant feedback from industry stakeholders over the coming weeks, and ERCOT intends to provide regular updates on this initiative to the Commission at open meetings.  ERCOT appreciates the willingness of Commission Staff to work with ERCOT in considering this study framework and the associated regulatory and legal mechanisms that will be necessary to effectuate it on a timely basis.  
Because the rulemaking in this project will establish many of the key elements of the interconnection process for large loads in the ERCOT Region, additional revisions to the discussion draft will likely be necessary to accommodate a batch study process.  ERCOT acknowledges that this interconnection standards project may or may not be the ideal vehicle for codifying this process, assuming it needs to be codified in Commission rules at all.  However, even if the batch study process is addressed through a separate rulemaking or an ERCOT revision request, ERCOT believes it would be beneficial to avoid creating a potential conflict with that concept in this interconnection standards rule, if that can be avoided. 
While ERCOT intends to pursue the batch study process as promptly as possible, ERCOT notes that it is only in the very beginning stages of developing this process, and so it may be difficult to definitively determine how that future process might conflict with the discussion draft of the proposed rule.  However, ERCOT’s present inclination is that the draft rule might present a conflict with a batch study concept in at least two respects: 
First, the discussion draft proposes that all interconnection studies will be performed by an electric utility.  ERCOT currently anticipates that its batch study proposal would involve a study by ERCOT, not by individual electric utilities, because the assessment in the batch study would consider the entire ERCOT Region—not just the TSP’s system and immediately adjacent areas, as is generally the case with large load interconnection studies.  The batch study in this respect is more akin to other planning-related studies that consider the entire ERCOT System, which ERCOT has historically been responsible for performing, given its system-wide purview.  Additional revisions to reflect ERCOT’s role in performing this study will likely be necessary.
Second, the discussion draft proposes that the large load customer need not satisfy arguably the most significant indicators of commitment—i.e., the financial commitment and CIAC requirements—until after the interconnection studies have been completed. While ERCOT currently envisions that a batch study process may include a preliminary study by the utility or ERCOT to provide the customer some initial indication of the feasibility of the load addition before the customer would be expected to provide its commitment, the value of the batch study concept depends on the basic precept that only those loads that have satisfied the most robust commitment criteria should be included in the study so that the results of the study accurately reflect the needs of the future ERCOT System.  ERCOT anticipates that adopting a batch study approach could require some revisions to the draft rule to provide that the criteria required in the discretionary services agreement and the intermediate agreement stages would need to be satisfied before the load would be fully evaluated in a batch study.  For purposes of the proposed CIAC specifically, ERCOT’s tentative expectation is that the cost amounts identified in an initial study or estimate could be increased or decreased based on the upgrades identified in the batch study.  This approach would require additional revisions.
Because there are a number of ways that the study process proposed in the discussion draft version could be modified to effectuate the purposes of the batch study process, which is still in the initial stages of development, ERCOT will refrain from offering specific revisions at this time in favor of further discussions with Commission Staff and industry stakeholders to determine the appropriate process. 
The draft rule should explicitly disclaim any purpose to preempt ERCOT’s interconnection processes except in the case of an explicit conflict.  
As noted above, ERCOT recently implemented PGRR 115, which formally created the large load interconnection process for the ERCOT Region in new Section 9 of the ERCOT Planning Guide.  PGRR 115 built on and improved the interim interconnection process that had been in place since March 2022.  ERCOT’s understanding is that Commission Staff generally intends the process described in the discussion draft to serve as an overlay to the process in Planning Guide Section 9, and not to entirely supplant it.  That intent would align with the fact that Section 9 establishes many requirements that are not reflected in the discussion draft rule and also provides a greater level of detail in many requirements than the rule does.  For example, Section 9 establishes processes for scoping the interconnection studies and for constructing the base cases for the various studies.  Because the draft rule establishes a chronological set of required steps that touch on many of the same essential areas of Planning Guide Section 9, including requirements for initiating the interconnection process, information that must be provided by the large load customer (or its interconnecting electric utility), and deadlines for taking certain actions, it may be helpful to foreclose any possible inference of an intent to preempt ERCOT’s interconnection framework—except to the extent of any express conflict—by explicitly disclaiming that purpose in the text of the rule.  For example, a statement such as “nothing in this section shall be construed to prohibit ERCOT from adopting requirements that are consistent with the express provisions of this section” would likely provide the necessary clarification.  
In some respects, the process described in the discussion draft appears to depart from the process established in Section 9 of ERCOT’s Planning Guide.  These provisions may present an express conflict that would require reconciliation in either the proposed rule or the Planning Guide.  For example, Planning Guide Section 9 provides that one condition for commencing the interconnection process is the “[s]ubmission of all information, including but not limited to, data required by the lead Transmission Service Provider (TSP) to perform steady state, short circuit, motor start, stability analyses and any other studies the lead TSP deems necessary to reliably interconnect the Load.”  The discussion draft rule does not contemplate such a condition and instead provides only that, “[n]ot later than 30 days after receipt of the required disclosures, financial commitment, and study fee required under subsection (c) of this section, the interconnecting electric utility must coordinate with ERCOT to conduct a large load interconnection study.”  If the discussion draft language is intended to establish all of the conditions for commencing the study scope discussion, the Commission may wish to consider whether the other conditions in Section 9.2.2 of the Planning Guide, including the provision of the required study data, should also be included in this provision. 
As another example, the draft rule requires that the proposed discretionary services agreement must be executed before the interconnecting electric utility submits its studies to ERCOT—presumably as a single study report.  By contrast, under the Planning Guide, which does not presently contemplate a discretionary service agreement, the lead TSP may send each of the large load interconnection study elements to ERCOT as that study element is completed.  If the Commission prefers this bundled study approach, ERCOT would need to revise its Planning Guide to foreclose separate submissions.  
Subsection (g) of the draft rule would require ERCOT to notify the interconnecting electric utility whether additional studies may be needed within 30 days of receiving the large load interconnection study from the interconnecting electric utility.  ERCOT is unclear whether this provision is intended to apply only to those additional studies that ERCOT might determine are needed based on its review of the utility’s interconnection studies (as contemplated in Planning Guide § 9.4(3)), or whether this is also intended to prohibit future studies that may be necessary due to factors such as changes in the large load’s project design, additions of “must-study” loads in the project area, or the evaluation of the large load’s characteristics with respect to newly identified reliability risks (such as a lack of voltage ride-through capability).  If the provision is intended to foreclose studies that may be justified by these other situations that could arise outside the scope of ERCOT’s review of the interconnection study, this would conflict with the ERCOT Planning Guide and could also present a reliability risk.  ERCOT notes that the problem of re-studies triggered by must-study loads is anticipated to be addressed by the forthcoming batch study process, as further discussed above.  Regardless of the purpose, ERCOT suggests that it may be helpful to clarify the intended scope of this provision.               
As detailed above, the rapid increase in the number of large loads seeking interconnection and ERCOT’s continued experience with the interconnection process has already prompted a re-examination of many aspects of this process, including the identified need for a batch study process.  As discussed at the December 18, 2025 open meeting, ERCOT aspires to implement the initial phase of this new batch process by the end of the first quarter in 2026, though the exact method of regulatory implementation remains an open issue.  However, it is still possible that the interconnection standards rule could take effect before the batch study process is implemented, and even following that implementation, it is likely that some aspects of the PGRR 115 process will continue to apply.  For these reasons, it may be helpful to ensure the rule does not inadvertently foreclose certain aspects of the interconnection process described in the Planning Guide.
ERCOT recommends including the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number as part of the information that must be submitted for “substantially similar” projects.
Section 37.0561(d) of PURA directs that the Commission’s interconnection standards must require a large load customer to provide information regarding substantially similar requests to its interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility.  That same provision implicitly recognizes that ERCOT may obtain information (including confidential information) about substantially similar requests when it excepts ERCOT and the Commission from the required prohibition against disclosure by the utility.  ERCOT agrees that having information on potentially duplicate facilities will be helpful to ERCOT’s planning assessments and related activities.  However, to maximize the value of this information, the customer should be required to provide the ERCOT-assigned serial number—the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number—so that the project can be uniquely (and more easily) identified. In some cases, an entity may be developing multiple projects of similar size in the same area, and having a unique identifier will allow ERCOT to more precisely identify these projects.  ERCOT therefore recommends revising subsections (c)(3)(A), (e)(3)(A), and (h)(3)(A) to require the customer to include the LLI number for each substantially similar project in the information provided to the interconnecting electric utility.  
 ERCOT recommends revisions to underscore its authority to require registration of large load customers.
ERCOT supports the Commission’s proposed inclusion of subsection (l), which further clarifies that ERCOT may establish operating standards for large load customers.  As the Commission is aware, ERCOT has sponsored Nodal Operating Guide Revision Request (NOGRR) 282 to establish voltage and frequency ride-through requirements for Large Electronic Loads (LELs)—i.e., large computing facilities such as data centers and cryptominers.  NOGRR 282 is essential to addressing a growing risk that LELs pose to the reliability of the ERCOT System.  These risks can only be fully mitigated by adopting requirements that ensure each large load customer protects the ERCOT grid from the reliability risks posed by that customer’s facilities.  The proposed language in the discussion draft provides helpful clarification of ERCOT’s authority to establish such standards when that is necessary to ensure system reliability.  
ERCOT would further recommend that the language be amended to explicitly recognize ERCOT’s authority to require large load customers to register with ERCOT.  This will be essential to ensure ERCOT has a direct line of communication with the customer when necessary to address voltage or frequency ride-through concerns.  It will also be necessary to ensure ERCOT has a communication pathway for each of the significant number of large load customers that will be subject to any of the various forms of curtailment contemplated under SB6.  Finally, as discussed at the December 18, 2025 open meeting, direct registration of large load customers will also ensure ERCOT can communicate directly with these customers during the interconnection process, allowing for a more accurate understanding of project status, rather than relying on an electric utility for all such communications.  Requiring large load customers to comply with ERCOT registration and operational requirements is consistent with SB6, which requires that the interconnection standards adopted by the Commission must be designed to support business development “while minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.”  
(l)	ERCOT operational standards.  
(1)	ERCOT may establish registration and operational standards for large load customers to ensure system reliability.  
(2)	A large load customer must comply with any registration or operational standards, developed through ERCOT protocols, as a condition for interconnection and continued operation of the customer’s load.

RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS
Question 1: Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request?  If so, how should the commission define those parameters? 
ERCOT Response:
The Commission’s discussion draft rule incorporates Senate Bill (SB) 6’s requirement that a large load customer “disclose to the interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility whether the customer is pursuing a substantially similar request for electric service in this state the approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the interconnection request.”  ERCOT believes the discussion draft includes the essential parameters prescribed by statute.  ERCOT does not necessarily oppose the use of other parameters but notes it may be difficult to identify other objective parameters that can easily help identify which projects exhibit the mutual exclusivity required by the statute, as ERCOT expects this will often be based on subjective factors known only to the large load customer (or a corporate parent or affiliate of that customer) such as the customer’s access to capital and the customer’s internal valuation of each project.  However, so long as any additional parameters imposed by the Commission are relevant to identifying that mutual exclusivity, those may be helpful to achieving the statutory purpose.
Question 2: Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details.  Should the commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive information)?  If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?
ERCOT Response:
ERCOT takes no position on whether the Commission should identify what information is competitively sensitive.  However, ERCOT notes that it has historically regarded information about individual large load interconnection projects as Protected Information pursuant to Section 1.3.1.1(1)(r) of the ERCOT Protocols, and in the absence of different direction from the Commission, ERCOT would continue to treat this information confidentially.  ERCOT’s comments on the proposed discussion draft rule recommend requiring the large load customer to provide the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number for any substantially similar projects—see I.C., above.  If the Commission agrees with this revision, it may wish to decide whether the LLI number should receive the same treatment as other information provided under subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3).
Question 3: Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed?  If only material changes, how should “material change” be defined?
ERCOT Response:
Section 9.2.3(1) of the ERCOT Planning Guide requires the interconnecting Transmission Service Provider to update a large load customer’s project information within ten Business Days of being notified by the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) of a “material change.”  Requiring the customer to notify the utility of any material change would be consistent with this requirement.  ERCOT suggests that the Commission may prefer to allow materiality to be determined on a case-by-case basis.  However, if the Commission prefers to define that term, ERCOT recommends that “material” be defined as “likely to have an impact on the findings of any interconnection study, the accurate modeling of the load, or the reliable operation of the load.”  
CONCLUSION
ERCOT appreciates the Commission’s consideration of these comments.  ERCOT would be pleased to discuss these issues with Commission Staff at the January 9, 2026 workshop or as may otherwise be convenient.

Date Signed: December 19, 2025
Respectfully submitted,

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ERCOT’S COMMENTS

Comments on Discussion Draft:
Consistent with ERCOT’s announcement at the Commission’s December 18, 2025 open meeting, ERCOT intends to develop a “batch study” proposal to replace the current interconnection study process that evaluates each large load addition individually.  This proposal is only in the early stages of development, but it is likely that such a process would require some revisions to the discussion draft of the interconnection standards rule to allow ERCOT to conduct the batch study and to require the most robust commitment criteria to be met before the batch study commences.  
ERCOT recommends that the Commission clarify that it does not intend to preempt ERCOT’s established interconnection process in Section 9 of the Planning Guide, except to the extent of any explicit conflict with the rule.  The Commission may wish to consider how best to reconcile several apparent conflicts between the proposed rule and the existing interconnection process.  If necessary, ERCOT can revise its Planning Guide to align with the final rule.
ERCOT recommends that the Commission revise the rule to require the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number ERCOT assigns each project to be included in the information required to be submitted for “substantially similar” projects.  This will allow ERCOT to more easily identify these projects.  
ERCOT supports the Commission’s proposed clarification regarding its authority to impose operational standards and recommends further revising subsection (l) to clarify that it may require large load customers to register directly with ERCOT.  
Responses to Commission Staff’s Questions:
Question 1: ERCOT sees no particular need to establish additional parameters to determine which projects are “substantially similar” but does not oppose new parameters that may be useful to identifying mutually exclusive projects. 
Question 2: Consistent with ERCOT’s recommended revision to include the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number in the list of information required to be submitted for “substantially similar” projects, the Commission may wish to clarify whether the LLI should be treated confidentially.  
Question 3: Requiring the large load customer to notify the utility of a material change would be consistent with the ERCOT Planning Guide, which requires the interconnecting TSP to notify ERCOT of any material change.  ERCOT recommends determining materiality on a case-by-case basis but has suggested language if the Commission wishes to define this in the rule.

interconnection study from the interconnecting electric utility. ERCOT is unclear whether this
provision is intended to apply only to those additional studies that ERCOT might determine are

         As detailed above, the rapid increase in the number of large loads seeking interconnection
and ERCOT's continued experience with the interconnection process has already prompted a re-
examination of many aspects of this process, including the identified need for a batch study
process. As discussed at the December 18,2025 open meeting, ERCOT aspires to implement the
initial phase of this new batch process by the end of the first quarter in 2026, though the exact
method of regulatory implementation remains an open issue. However, it is still possible that the
interconnection standards rule could take effect before the batch study process is implemented,
and even following that implementation, it is likely that some aspects of the PGRR 115 process
will continue to apply. For these reasons, it may be helpful to ensure the rule does not inadvertently
foreclose certain aspects ofthe interconnection process described in the Planning Guide.

require a large load customer to provide information regarding substantially similar requests to its
interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility.            That same provision implicitly
recognizes that ERCOT may obtain information (including confidential information) about
substantially similar requests when it excepts ERCOT and the Commission from the required

activities. However, to maximize the value of this information, the customer should be required
to provide the ERCOT-assigned serial number-the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number-

              D. ERCOT recommends revisions to underscore its authority to require
                  registration of large load customers.

           ERCOT supports the Commission' s proposed inclusion of subsection (l), which further
clarifies that ERCOT may establish operating standards for large load customers.           As the
Commission is aware, ERCOT has sponsored Nodal Operating Guide Revision Request (NOGRR)
282 to establish voltage and frequency ride-through requirements for Large Electronic Loads
(LELs)-i.e., large computing facilities such as data centers and cryptominers. 11 NOGRR 282 is
essential to addressing a growing risk that LELs pose to the reliability of the ERCOT System.
These risks can only be fully mitigated by adopting requirements that ensure each large load
customer protects the ERCOT grid from the reliability risks posed by that customer' s facilities.
The proposed language in the discussion draft provides helpful clarification ofERCOT's authority
to establish such standards when that is necessary to ensure system reliability.

           ERCOT would further recommend that the language be amended to explicitly recognize
ERCOT's authority to require large load customers to register with ERCOT. This will be essential
to ensure ERCOT has a direct line of communication with the customer when necessary to address
voltage or frequency ride-through concerns. It will also be necessary to ensure ERCOT has a
communication pathway for each of the significant number of large load customers that will be
subject to any of the various forms of curtailment contemplated under SB6. Finally, as discussed

II.     RESPONSES TO QUESTIONS

Question 1: Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how should the
commission define those parameters?
ERCOT Response:

        The Commission's discussion draft rule incorporates Senate Bill (SB) 6's requirement that
a large load customer "disclose to the interconnecting electric utility or municipally owned utility
whether the customer is pursuing a substantially similar request for electric service in this state the
approval of which would result in the customer materially changing, delaying, or withdrawing the
interconnection request."13 ERCOT believes the discussion draft includes the essential parameters
prescribed by statute. ERCOT does not necessarily oppose the use of other parameters but notes
it may be difficult to identify other objective parameters that can easily help identify which projects
exhibit the mutual exclusivity required by the statute, as ERCOT expects this will often be based
on subjective factors known only to the large load customer (or a corporate parent or affiliate of

12 PURA § 37.0561(b).
13 See proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(d); Tex. Util. Code § 37.0561(d).

                                                       8
 that customer) such as the customer' s access to capital and the customer' s internal valuation of
each project. However, so long as any additional parameters imposed by the Commission are
relevant to identifying that mutual exclusivity, those may be helpful to achieving the statutory
purpose.

Question 2: Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows a large
load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the commission list what
is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not competitively sensitive
information)? If so, what information should and should not be considered competitively
sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and ERCOT can identify whether there is a
duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to materialize?
ERCOT Response:

        ERCOT takes no position on whether the Commission should identify what information is
competitively sensitive.   However, ERCOT notes that it has historically regarded information
about individual large load interconnection projects as Protected Information pursuant to Section
1.3.1.1(1)(r) of the ERCOT Protocols, and in the absence of different direction from the
Commission, ERCOT would continue to treat this information confidentially.             ERCOT's
comments on the proposed discussion draft rule recommend requiring the large load customer to
provide the Large Load Interconnection (LLI) number for any substantially similar projects-see
I.C., above. If the Commission agrees with this revision, it may wish to decide whether the LLI
number should receive the same treatment as other information provided under subsections (c)(3),
(e)(3), and (h)(3).

Question 3: Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the
interconnecting electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially
disclosed in response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If
only material changes, how should "material change" be defined?
ERCOT Response:

        Section 9.2.3(1) ofthe ERCOT Planning Guide requires the interconnecting Transmission
Service Provider to update a large load customer's project information within ten Business Days
of being notified by the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (ILLE) of a "material change."
Requiring the customer to notify the utility of any material change would be consistent with this
requirement.    ERCOT suggests that the Commission may prefer to allow materiality to be
determined on a case-by-case basis. However, if the Commission prefers to define that term,


                                                9
 ERCOT recommends that "material" be defined as "likely to have an impact on the findings of
any interconnection study, the accurate modeling of the load, or the reliable operation of the load."

                   EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF ERCOT'S COMMENTS

Comments on Discussion Draft:

   •   Consistent with ERCOT's announcement at the Commission's December 18, 2025 open meeting,
       ERCOT intends to develop a "batch study" proposal to replace the current interconnection study
       process that evaluates each large load addition individually. This proposal is only in the early
       stages of development, but it is likely that such a process would require some revisions to the
       discussion draft of the interconnection standards rule to allow ERCOT to conduct the batch study
       and to require the most robust commitment criteria to be met before the batch study commences.

   •   ERCOT recommends that the Commission clarify that it does not intend to preempt ERCOT's
       established interconnection process in Section 9 of the Planning Guide, except to the extent of any
       explicit conflict with the rule. The Commission may wish to consider how best to reconcile several
       apparent conflicts between the proposed rule and the existing interconnection process. Ifnecessary,
       ERCOT can revise its Planning Guide to align with the final rule.

   •   ERCOT recommends that the Commission revise the rule to require the Large Load Interconnection
       (LLI) number ERCOT assigns each project to be included in the information required to be
       submitted for "substantially similar" projects. This will allow ERCOT to more easily identify these
       projects.

   •   ERCOT supports the Commission's proposed clarification regarding its authority to impose
       operational standards and recommends further revising subsection (l) to clarify that it may require
       large load customers to register directly with ERCOT.

   •   Question 1: ERCOT sees no particular need to establish additional parameters to determine which
       projects are "substantially similar" but does not oppose new parameters that may be useful to
       identifying mutually exclusive projects.

   •   Question 2: Consistent with ERCOT's recommended revision to include the Large Load
       Interconnection (LLI) number in the list of information required to be submitted for "substantially
       similar" projects, the Commission may wish to clarify whether the LLI should be treated
       confidentially.

   •   Question 3: Requiring the large load customer to notify the utility of a material change would be
       consistent with the ERCOT Planning Guide, which requires the interconnecting TSP to notify
       ERCOT of any material change. ERCOT recommends determining materiality on a case-by-case
       basis but has suggested language ifthe Commission wishes to define this in the rule.
